sections.h2: What should a seller know about North Carolina before opening a local guide?
sections.html:
North Carolina sales run through county offices at nearly every step. The assessor values the parcel, the tax collector bills it, the register of deeds records the sale, and the clerk of superior court handles foreclosures and estates. This overview shows how those offices fit together so you know whom to call first in your county.

Some rules are the same in every county, such as the recording fee schedule and the deed excise rate. Others change with the county: tax rates, appeal calendars, relief application hours and courthouse procedures. The county and city guides on this site pick up where this statewide summary stops.

sections.h2: How big is the North Carolina housing market?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau counts 11,197,968 residents in North Carolina on July 1, 2025, which is 7.2% above the April 2020 estimates base. That growth feeds a large housing stock, and the figures below are statewide medians from QuickFacts.

  • Housing units on July 1, 2025: 5,168,052.
  • Owner-occupied housing unit rate, 2020 to 2024: 66.6%.
  • Median value of owner-occupied housing units, 2020 to 2024: $288,900.
  • Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024: $1,228.
  • Median monthly owner costs: $1,631 with a mortgage and $490 without one.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 86,167.
  • Residents aged 65 and over: 18.9%.

A statewide median hides wide gaps between a mountain county, a coastal county and a Triangle suburb. Ask the county tax office for the appraised value and tax history of the specific parcel you plan to sell.

sections.h2: How different are North Carolina counties from each other?
sections.html:
They differ a great deal in size and age. The state's county directory gives areas that run from 221 square miles in Clay County to 1,562 square miles in Dare County.

The oldest entries date to 1668 (Chowan, Currituck, Pasquotank and Perquimans), and the newest are Avery and Hoke, both formed in 1911. In several counties the courthouse sits in a small town and not in the largest city, so a trip to record a deed or file an estate can mean a longer drive than the map suggests. Check the county seat before you plan a signing.

sections.h2: Where is a North Carolina deed recorded, and what does recording cost?
sections.html:
A deed is recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the land lies, and each county elects that official every two years. Recording is the step that makes a transfer effective against outside parties.

  • Excise tax: $1.00 on each $500 of consideration or value, or fractional part of $500, paid by the person transferring the property before the deed is recorded.
  • Recording fee for most instruments: $26.00 for the first 15 pages and $4.00 for each extra page.
  • Recording fee for a deed of trust or mortgage: $64.00 for the first 35 pages and $4.00 for each extra page.
  • Satisfactions and cancellations of a deed of trust or mortgage: no recording fee.

State law says an unrecorded conveyance, option or lease longer than three years does not bind lien creditors or buyers who paid value, and priority follows the order in which instruments are registered. For a seller, that means a clean, prompt recording protects the buyer and avoids disputes later.

sections.h2: When is North Carolina property tax listed, due and appealed?
sections.html:
The calendar is set by statute and applies to all counties, though the commissioners can shift some of it. These are the points that matter most when a sale falls near a deadline.

  • Listing opens on the first business day of January and ends January 31.
  • Taxes are due September 1 and are payable at face amount through January 5.
  • Interest of 2% starts on January 6, then three-fourths of one percent a month from February 1 until the bill is paid.
  • The county board of equalization and review first meets between the first Monday in April and the first Monday in May.
  • A further appeal goes to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days after the county board mails its decision.
  • Every county must reappraise real property at least once every eighth year.

Counties with 75,000 or more people can be forced to reappraise sooner if their sales assessment ratio falls below .85 or climbs above 1.15. Ask your county assessor which year your parcel was last revalued.

sections.h2: What do North Carolina household figures say about buyers and sellers?
sections.html:
QuickFacts counts 4,282,345 households for 2020 to 2024, averaging 2.44 persons each, and 87.3% of residents aged one year or older lived in the same house a year earlier. Median household income was $72,388 in 2024 dollars, and workers spent a mean of 25.1 minutes getting to work.

Read together, those numbers describe a state where most people stay put. Sellers of long-held homes can carry old repairs, unrecorded family transfers or estate paperwork, and that is why the statewide probate and tax guides sit beside the county pages.

sections.h2: Which North Carolina office handles foreclosure, probate and eviction?
sections.html:
Foreclosure, probate and eviction all start with the courts, though not the same room. North Carolina uses power-of-sale foreclosure, so the clerk of superior court holds the hearing in the county where the house stands, and notice must be served at least 10 days before it. After a sale, anyone can file an upset bid within 10 days if it tops the last price by at least 5% and at least $750.

Estates go to the elected clerk of superior court, who acts as probate judge. Evictions are filed in small claims before a magistrate, with a hearing usually set within 10 to 15 days, and an appeal to district court must be noted within 10 days of the ruling. Our statewide pages on probate, landlord and tenant law, and the homestead exclusion explain each process in more detail.

sections.h2: How do the guides for North Carolina fit together?
sections.html:
The statewide guides explain the law once: probate, foreclosure, eviction, tax sales, squatters and the elderly or disabled exclusion. County guides then cover the register of deeds in that county and its property tax process, and city guides describe selling a house in a particular town.

If you are not sure which applies, begin with the county where the property sits, because that county sets the tax bill, holds the deed records and runs the clerk's office. A sale that crosses two counties is recorded in the county holding the greater value for excise tax purposes, so confirm that with the register of deeds before closing.

faqs.q: How many people live in North Carolina?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimated 11,197,968 residents on July 1, 2025. That is a 7.2% rise from the April 2020 estimates base of 10,441,392.

faqs.q: Who records a deed in North Carolina?
faqs.a: The register of deeds in the county where the land is located records it. The person transferring the property pays the excise tax to that office before recording.

faqs.q: When are North Carolina property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due September 1. They can be paid at face amount before January 6, and interest begins that day.

faqs.q: Where do I appeal a property valuation in North Carolina?
faqs.a: Start with your county board of equalization and review, which first meets between early April and early May. If you disagree with its decision, you can appeal to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days of the mailed notice.

faqs.q: Which court handles a North Carolina foreclosure?
faqs.a: The clerk of superior court in the county where the property sits holds the hearing. Foreclosure here is by power of sale, with at least 10 days of notice before the hearing.
